paras: The threatened lynching of Tone Wiggins took place in the Mt. Pleasant section of Nash County, North Carolina, in late August 1900, after Wiggins, a Black man, was arrested on suspicion of shooting a white farmer, Manoah M. Bissett. A dispatch reprinted in three white newspapers reported "threats of lynching the negro" while he was being tried, but described no move against him and gave no outcome.

On a Friday night, Bissett, described as "a prominent farmer" of the section, was disturbed by a noise at his barn and went out to investigate but found nothing. As he turned from the barn a shotgun was fired, and he was struck by nineteen small shot, twelve in the head and seven in the shoulder; the wounds were called severe but not expected to be fatal. Because Bissett had "the reputation of being a peaceable man," the dispatch said, it was hard to find a cause for the shooting.

Suspicion fell on Wiggins, who worked in that section, and he was arrested. On the morning of August 27 his trial was held at Bissett's house, since Bissett was too badly wounded to leave it. The dispatch closed with a single sentence, "There are threats of lynching the negro," without saying who made the threats or how.
No report of the result of the hearing, of any attempt on Wiggins, or of Bissett's recovery appears in the coverage.

The Raleigh News & Observer printed the story first, on August 29, under the headline "NINETEEN SHOT STRUCK. Attempted Assassination in Nashville. Narrow Escape from Death." The next day the Norfolk Virginian-Pilot ran the same text as "a special from Nashville" inside its Raleigh letter, under "ATTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE" and the deck line "A Peaceable Farmer Shot in the Dark," giving the accused's name as Tom Wiggins. On September 4 the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger reprinted it from the Charlotte Observer under a Goldsboro dateline, among other state news items.

All three versions framed the episode as an attack on a respected white farmer, identified Wiggins only as "a negro man," and mentioned the lynching threats in passing without comment. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The copies differ on the accused's first name, "Tone" in the News & Observer and the Messenger and "Tom" in the Virginian-Pilot, and on the dateline, Nashville in two copies and Goldsboro in the third.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Tone Wiggins
bases: All three copies of one report say a Black man arrested for shooting a white farmer faced 'threats of lynching', with no act against him reported (A1, A2, A3).
The report mentions only 'threats of lynching the negro' after Wiggins was accused of the shooting; no one is reported killed and no group or act is described (A1, A2, A3).
The three articles print one dispatch nearly word for word (A1, A2, A3), so there is a single account, not independent corroboration.

accounts.label: Nashville/Goldsboro special dispatch
accounts.gist: Bissett was shot as he turned from his barn on a Friday night; suspicion fell on Wiggins, who was arrested and tried at Bissett's house, and there were threats of lynching him.

framing.detail: The Raleigh News & Observer headlined 'NINETEEN SHOT STRUCK. Attempted Assassination in Nashville', stressed Bissett's good name, and noted the lynching threats in one closing sentence without comment.

The Virginian-Pilot ran the special under 'ATTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE' in a Raleigh column ('A Peaceable Farmer Shot in the Dark'), and the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger reprinted it from the Charlotte Observer among state news.

conflicts.note: Two of the three copies, including the first printed, give 'Tone'; the difference may be a typesetting change.
Same text under two datelines; the Nashville version is the one placed nearest the scene.
